36.title: The sleeping palace
36.hook: he wakes at night to see the musicians asleep and sprawled; the glamour is gone
36.howItsDone: Buddhists retell the sleeping palace as the night of the great departure, and teachers point to samvega, the jolt of seeing life plainly, as a healthy spur to practice rather than a reason for gloom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rahula: a son is born, and his name means a fetter. Your line was love, and the fear inside it. Did you loosen your grip by one finger? Day thirty-six, and a new week: the going forth.
screen: `RAHULA — LOVE, AND THE FEAR INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: The end of a party, two in the morning. The lights come up. The music stops. The room that looked magical an hour ago is suddenly just a room: sticky cups, a torn streamer, someone asleep on the couch with their mouth open. Nothing has changed except the light, and yet everything has. In the story, the prince comes home on the night his son is born. The palace throws him a celebration: dancers, singers, musicians, all for him. But his mind is somewhere else, and he falls asleep in the middle of it. The performers, seeing no one watching, lie down where they are and sleep too. Sometime in the night, the prince wakes up. Today, the sleeping palace.
screen: `THE LIGHTS COME UP.` → `A PARTY FOR THE PRINCE.` → `HE WAKES IN THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The lamps are still burning, and by their light he sees his palace as it really is. The later telling doesn't spare the details. Dancers sprawled across the floor, instruments dropped beside them. Some snoring. Some grinding their teeth. Some talking in their sleep, mouths open, clothes in disarray. The same people who were beautiful and dazzling a few hours ago are just tired bodies now. The telling says the great hall looked to him like a burial ground. And earlier that same evening, one more thing happened. A young woman watching him ride by had sung a little verse: happy is the mother, happy the father, happy the wife of a man like this. The word she used for happy can also mean cooled, at peace, and it's related to nibbana. The prince heard it and thought: what is it that's truly cooled? And he knew. The fires of wanting, gone out. Put those two moments together and you have today's teaching. The glamour was never in the palace. It was a spell, a way of seeing, and in one night it broke. Buddhists have a word for this feeling, samvega: a jolt of clear-eyed urgency, the shock of seeing ordinary life plainly. It isn't disgust with people. The dancers did nothing wrong. It's the moment the prince stops being enchanted, and starts being awake to what he'd been looking at all along.

segments.voice: Look around the room you're in right now, as if the lights just came up. Pick one ordinary thing: a chair, a lamp, a pile of laundry, a phone. Look at it as if you've never seen it before. Its shape. Its color. What it's for. What it cost, what it will become when it wears out. You're not trying to dislike anything. You're just seeing it without the story you usually tell about it. Then close your eyes and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Samvega. The jolt of clear-eyed urgency the prince felt waking to see his glittering hall by plain lamplight, the spell of it gone.
Your line: the spell breaks. Today, see one familiar room with fresh eyes, your kitchen, your desk, your car, and notice what's actually there. Day thirty-six.

37.title: One look back
37.hook: he looks in on Yasodhara and the baby and does not wake them
37.howItsDone: Buddhists tell the great going forth as the moment of renunciation, and many honor Yasodhara's part in it; the scene is often painted in temple murals, the prince standing at the door of the sleeping room.

segments.voice: Yesterday, samvega: the prince woke to see the glittering hall by plain lamplight. Your line was the spell breaks. Which room did you see with fresh eyes? Day thirty-seven.

A doorway at night. A child's room, maybe, or a parent's, or someone you loved who was sleeping. You stand there a moment longer than you need to. You don't go in. You don't say anything. You just look. The prince has decided. Tonight he will leave the palace. He has told Channa to saddle his horse. But before he goes, there is one more door he has to stand in. Down the corridor is the room where Yasodhara sleeps, with their newborn son beside her. Today, one look back.
screen: `A DOORWAY AT NIGHT.` → `THE DECISION IS MADE.` → `ONE MORE DOOR.`

segments.voice: In the later telling, he opens the door quietly. A lamp is burning. Yasodhara is asleep on a bed strewn with flowers, and her hand is resting on the baby's head. The prince stands on the threshold and wants, more than anything, to hold his son. But to lift the child, he would have to move her hand, and she would wake. And if she woke, he knew he could not go. So he stays in the doorway. The telling gives him one thought: when I have found what I'm looking for, I will come back and see my son. And he closes the door. It's a tender scene, and it's also one people argue about. Some readers today feel the ache of it: a husband and father walking out at night without a word. Buddhists hold the story in different ways. Some see it as a great sacrifice, made for the sake of everyone, including this family. Others say plainly that it's hard, and that the story's honesty about the cost matters. The later stories add that Yasodhara, when she learns he has gone to live simply, gives up her own jewels and fine clothes, and that one day both she and Rahula will walk the same path. What the scene knows, whatever you make of the leaving, is how the hardest goodbyes happen. Not with speeches. In silence, from a doorway, with a hand on the frame. The Pali word for what he's choosing is nekkhamma, renunciation, and the story never pretends it's easy.

Your line: the hardest leaving is quiet. Today, if a goodbye comes, even a small one at a door or a bus stop, let yourself look a moment longer. Day thirty-seven.

38.title: Channa and Kanthaka
38.hook: the charioteer and the white horse ride out at midnight through the city gate
38.howItsDone: Temple murals and carvings across the Buddhist world show the great departure, the prince on the white horse Kanthaka with Channa holding its tail, and some festivals reenact the ride.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nekkhamma: the prince in the doorway, not waking Yasodhara and the baby. Your line was the hardest leaving is quiet. Did you let a goodbye last a moment longer? Day thirty-eight.

Who drove you to the airport the first time you really left home? Who sat in the waiting room with you, or helped carry the boxes up three flights of stairs? Most big journeys in a life have someone at the very start of them, someone who doesn't come all the way, but gets you out the door. The prince has one too. Two, in fact. It's midnight. The palace is asleep. In the stable courtyard, his charioteer, Channa, is holding the reins of a great white horse named Kanthaka. The prince swings up into the saddle. Channa takes hold of the horse's tail. And the three of them head for the city gate. Today, Channa and Kanthaka.
screen: `WHO DROVE YOU TO THE AIRPORT?` → `MIDNIGHT IN THE STABLE YARD.` → `THREE HEAD FOR THE GATE.`

segments.voice: The later telling makes this ride glow. Kanthaka is enormous and pure white, and the tradition says both he and Channa were born on the very same day as the prince. So this is no hired driver and borrowed horse. These are the companions of his whole life. The telling says the gods muffled the sound of Kanthaka's hooves with their hands so no one would wake. The city gate, so heavy it took many men to open, swung open by itself. And at the gate, a figure appears in the air: Mara, the tempter. Turn back, he says. In seven days, you'll be king of the whole world. The prince doesn't even slow down. Mara will be back in this story, and he's patient. But tonight the three ride on, and by dawn, the telling says, they've crossed three kingdoms. Now step back from the wonders for a moment. Whatever you make of muffled hooves and opening gates, the heart of the scene is simple and human. The prince did not leave alone. Channa, who had answered his questions honestly on the road to the park, now helps him go, knowing it means losing him. Kanthaka carries him as far as a horse can. Every tradition of the story keeps them, and Buddhists remember them with real affection. Great journeys are often told as solo adventures. This one isn't. The going forth, the most famous departure in Buddhism, begins with a friend holding a horse's tail in the dark.

A teacher who opened a door, a stranger who gave you directions when you were lost. Picture their face. Remember the moment, the car, the room, the road. Then, silently or out loud, say thank you. If you can, decide to tell them today. If you can't, let the thanks be enough. The bell holds the time.

Your line: someone rode with you. Today, thank one person who got you somewhere, with a message, a call, or a word in person. Day thirty-eight.

39.title: The cut hair
39.hook: at the river Anoma he cuts his hair with his sword and puts on a simple robe
39.howItsDone: In Theravada novice ordination, called pabbajja, the head is shaved and a robe put on; in Myanmar, boys going through shinbyu are dressed as princes before being robed as novices for a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kanthaka: the white horse, with Channa alongside, who carried the prince out at midnight. Your line was someone rode with you. Who did you thank? Day thirty-nine.

Have you ever cut your hair after something ended? A breakup, a new job, a hard year. The mirror shows someone lighter, someone starting over. Hair can carry who we've been. By dawn, the three riders reach a river. The later telling names it the Anoma. The prince gets down from Kanthaka on the sandy bank. He's still dressed as what he was: a prince, in silk and jewels, with long hair bound up in a royal topknot. He draws his sword. Channa watches. Today's word is what happens next.
screen: `HAIR IS WHO WE'VE BEEN.` → `DAWN AT THE RIVER.` → `HE DRAWS HIS SWORD.`

segments.voice: He takes his long hair in one hand and cuts through it with the sword. In the telling, what's left is short, curling to the right, and it stays that length for the rest of his life. Tradition links this to the small tight curls on statues of the Buddha. He throws the topknot into the air. Then he takes off his royal clothes and puts on a simple robe, the color of earth, like the wanderer from the fourth sight. He gives his jewels to Channa to take home. And in that moment, the prince is gone. There's a samana on the riverbank. The word for this is pabbajja. It means going forth: leaving the household life for the homeless one. It's still the word for it. In Theravada communities, when someone becomes a novice monk or nun, the ceremony is called pabbajja, and the head is shaved, as on that riverbank. In Myanmar, there's a ceremony for boys called shinbyu: they're first dressed up as princes, in silk and makeup, and paraded through town, and then their heads are shaved and they put on robes for a time, retelling this very morning with their own lives. What pabbajja teaches, even for people who never shave a head, is that some things we carry are costumes. The prince didn't hate his hair or his jewels. He just didn't need them for where he was going. There was simply less to carry.

40.title: Kanthaka's heart
40.hook: a later telling: the horse, sent home without him, dies of grief
40.howItsDone: Buddhists extend the first precept, not killing, to animals, and the loving-kindness practice of the Metta Sutta wishes well to all beings, seen and unseen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pabbajja: the going forth, the hair cut with a sword on the riverbank. Your line was less to carry. What small vanity did you set down? Day forty.

A horse can't be told why. On the riverbank at dawn, the prince, now in his plain robe, turns to Channa and gives his orders. Go home. Take the jewels. Take Kanthaka. Tell my family I'm well. Channa begs to go forth with him. The prince says no. The words are meant for Channa, but the white horse is standing right there, reins slack, and the telling says he hears every one of them. If a dog has ever watched you pack a suitcase, you've seen a small version of this: the ears drop, the eyes follow you to the door. Today, Kanthaka's heart.
screen: `A HORSE CAN'T BE TOLD WHY.` → `GO HOME, CHANNA.` → `THE HORSE HEARS IT ALL.`

segments.voice: This part comes from the later tellings, not the suttas. In one version, Kanthaka kneels and licks his master's feet, weeping. In the Pali telling, Kanthaka understands he will never see his master again. He walks away with Channa, and as the prince passes out of sight, the horse's heart breaks, and he dies right there on the road. Channa goes home alone, with two griefs to carry. And then the story does something tender. It says Kanthaka was reborn among the gods, in a heavenly realm, as a being named Kanthaka, because of his love and his service. The horse's grief wasn't wasted. Why would Buddhists keep a story like this? Because in the Buddhist view, animals aren't scenery. They're sentient beings, beings who feel, who can suffer, who can love. The first precept, to refrain from killing, reaches to them. The Buddha's teaching on loving-kindness wishes happiness to all beings, the weak and the strong, the seen and the unseen. And in the Jataka stories of his past lives, the Buddha-to-be is again and again an animal: a monkey, a deer, a hare, an elephant. Kanthaka's heart puts the same thing in one image: in this story, love is not only a human thing. When we leave, they grieve too. Whether or not you take the heavenly rebirth literally, the story asks you to take the grief seriously.

Remember what it gave without asking for anything. If you'd like, silently wish it well: may you be happy, may you be free from fear. The bell holds the time.
Kanthaka's heart. The white horse who, in the later telling, died of grief when his master sent him home, and was reborn among the gods.

41.title: The king's offer
41.hook: in Rajagaha King Bimbisara offers him wealth; he declines (Sn 3.1), and later tradition adds his promise to return if he finds the way
41.howItsDone: Buddhists remember King Bimbisara as one of the Buddha's great lay supporters, and the Pabbajja Sutta, the poem of this meeting, is still recited and studied as an early account of the going forth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kanthaka's heart: the white horse who, in the later telling, died of grief. Your line was they grieve too. Which animal did you treat gently? Day forty-one.

Rajagaha, capital of the kingdom of Magadha. A stranger with a shaved head walks from house to house with a bowl, eyes lowered, taking whatever is put in it. From his palace, King Bimbisara sees him, and something in the way this man walks makes the king send messengers after him. Turning down something bad is easy. Turning down something good, more money, a promotion, a place in someone's big plans, is a different kind of hard. That's what's coming on a hillside outside the city. Today, the king's offer.
screen: `A STRANGER WITH A BOWL.` → `THE KING WATCHES FROM ABOVE.` → `SAYING NO TO SOMETHING GOOD.`

segments.voice: This scene is in the Pali canon itself, in a poem in the Sutta Nipata called the Going Forth. The king notices that this beggar is no ordinary beggar. He walks mindfully, the poem says, eyes down, looking only a yoke's length ahead. His messengers find him on a hill outside the city, eating his alms food, and the king comes out in his chariot to meet him. And the king makes an offer. You're young, you're clearly of noble birth. Come and lead my army. Take wealth. Enjoy it. The wanderer answers calmly. He tells the king where he comes from: a people of the Himalayan foothills, the Sakyans. He says he didn't leave home looking for pleasures. He's seen the danger in them, and he sees safety in letting them go. I'm going to strive, he says. That's where my heart is. The poem ends there. The later commentaries add one more exchange, and it's the one people remember. The king says: then when you find what you're looking for, come back here first and teach me. And the wanderer promises he will. Tradition says he kept that promise, and the story will get there. What the scene shows is a no that isn't rude, bitter or proud. He declines a kingdom, kindly, and leaves the door open. A promise to come back is a way of saying: this no isn't about you. It's about the road.

42.title: Two teachers
42.hook: he masters the deep states taught by Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta, and leaves: good, but not the end (MN 26)
42.howItsDone: Buddhist meditators still study the deep absorptions and formless states, and teachers often tell the story of the two teachers to show that calm states, however deep, are a means rather than the goal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bimbisara offered wealth and an army, and the wanderer said no, kindly. Your line was a promise to come back. What did you decline? Day forty-two, the last day of the going forth.

What comes after getting good at something? Years on a language, an instrument, a craft. People start coming to you for advice. And then, right at the top of it, a quiet question can show up anyway: is this it? Not because the thing is bad. Because it isn't what you came for. The wanderer has left the palace to find an answer to age, sickness and death, and in his world there are teachers of meditation with communities of students around them. He goes to the first. Today, two teachers.

segments.voice: This story comes from the Buddha himself, in a sutta where he looks back on his search. His first teacher was Alara Kalama. Alara taught a meditation that led to a very deep state called the base of nothingness: a mind so still that it rests in nothing at all. The wanderer learned it fast. Soon he could reach it himself. Alara was delighted, and did something generous. He said, you know what I know. Let's lead this community together, as equals. And the wanderer thought about it and said no. Why? Because, he says, this teaching doesn't lead to the end of suffering. It leads only to that state. When you come out of it, you're still you, with everything you carried in. So he went to a second teacher, Uddaka Ramaputta, whose father had taught an even subtler state: neither perception nor non-perception, a stillness so fine it can barely be described. Again he mastered it. Again he was offered leadership, this time the whole community. Again he said no, and walked away. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say these teachers were frauds or these states were useless. Buddhists still teach these deep meditative states today, and later suttas list them among the attainments of meditation. What he says is simpler. Good, but not the end. That's this week, the going forth, in one line: samvega, the doorway, the midnight ride, the cut hair, a horse's grief, Bimbisara's offer, and two teachers. Every time, something good is left behind, because it isn't the end.
screen: `ALARA — THE BASE OF NOTHINGNESS.` · `LET'S LEAD TOGETHER. NO.` · `UDDAKA — SUBTLER STILL. NO.` · `NOT FRAUDS. JUST NOT THE END.` · then, large: `GOOD, BUT NOT THE END.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of one thing you've learned well. A skill, a subject, a habit, a practice. Give it its due for a breath or two: the hours it took, the work it was. Then ask it, gently: what's next? Not to throw it away. Just to see if there's a further step. A deeper question. Something it points toward. Don't rush for an answer. Just let the question sit beside the skill. The bell holds the time.
Two teachers. Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta, who taught the wanderer deep meditative states, and whom he left because the states were good, but not the end.
